answer.rationale: The finance mandate is binding, the incumbent has refused to reopen price, and memory_c2 documents that the low-cost vendor was previously onboarded quickly with accurate invoicing and sharp unit-cost reduction. The 14-day expiry with no auto-renewal creates a hard deadline that rules out defer_decision. Adding a second source or negotiating terms are blocked: the incumbent won't move on price, and dual-sourcing adds cost pressure we cannot absorb under the 18% cut. memory_c6's multi-year lesson is directionally consistent (longer term, lower cost) and can be layered into the new contract structure with the low-cost vendor without widening scope. The single verification I choose is memory_c2 because the entire case hinges on whether the low-cost vendor's past performance was genuinely clean (quick onboarding, accurate invoicing) or whether the summary hides integration or quality issues that would raise delivery risk at 94% line utilization. If the archive confirms c2 as recorded, I commit to switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor, locking in the quoted price that meets the 18% mandate alone, and structuring the agreement as a multi-year commitment to extend the cost benefit per c6. Delivery-risk mitigation: I would require the incumbent to honor the current contract through its final day and stage the new vendor's first delivery overlapping the last incumbent shipment window so there is no gap at the assembly line. No second source is added this cycle; that remains in the queue for the next review if the line rate drops further. If c2 verification surfaces material risk not captured in the summary, I would fall back to renew_incumbent at existing terms and escalate the finance gap rather than accept delivery risk.
